analysis.one_liner: Lets college athletes profit from their names, images, and likenesses, and guarantees scholarships and injury coverage.
analysis.headline: Introduced in the final two weeks of the 116th Congress with two House sponsors, the bill was referred to two committees and died without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: College athletes generate billions for universities, athletic conferences, and the NCAA, but have historically been barred from earning money from their own fame. This bill would have let them sign endorsement deals and hire agents, forced colleges and athletic associations to share revenue with athletes in big-money sports, guaranteed scholarships through graduation, created a medical trust fund for sports injuries, and set federal health and safety rules for athletic programs. It never advanced past committee referral before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: College athletes, especially those in revenue-producing sports like football and basketball. They could sell their names, images, and likenesses without penalty to their scholarships, transfer schools without sitting out, get independent medical second opinions, keep scholarships through degree completion even after their playing days end, and receive annual royalty payments from the revenue their sports generate. Former athletes could get out-of-pocket injury costs covered for five years after leaving school, and conditions like chronic traumatic encephalopathy would be covered [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: College athletes, especially football and basketball players

how_it_helps.text: Bars universities, conferences, and the NCAA from restricting athletes' ability to market their names, images, likenesses, or athletic reputations, and ensures such earnings do not count against financial aid eligibility [S2][S3].

Requires revenue sharing: institutions in divisions where program revenue exceeds scholarship spending must transfer 50% of that revenue (minus scholarship costs) to the athletic association for distribution among eligible athletes, with public disclosure of the amounts [S3].
Guarantees a scholarship through graduation even if the athlete stops playing, and bars revocation because the athlete signed an endorsement contract [S3].

Creates a medical trust fund covering out-of-pocket sports injury costs, certain sports-related conditions like chronic traumatic encephalopathy, and independent medical second opinions, funded by a 2.5% to 4% levy on athletic department revenue [S2][S3].

Directs the CDC to set health and safety guidelines covering concussions, cardiac health, mental health, and sexual violence, with fines of up to 30% of athletic revenue for noncompliance, and requires trainers to be independent of the athletic department [S2][S3].

Lets athletes transfer schools without losing eligibility or scholarships, enter professional drafts without losing college eligibility, and obtain agent representation, and creates a Commission on College Athletics with a hotline, ombudsman, and private right of action to enforce these rights [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: The NCAA, athletic conferences, and big-college athletic departments would bear the cost: up to 50% of program revenue redirected to athletes, annual contributions to the medical trust fund, civil penalties of 15-30% of athletic revenue for violations, and fees for associations with revenues over $20 million. The bill authorizes $50 million in appropriations for the new Commission in each of fiscal 2021 and 2022 [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: The NCAA, conferences, and college athletic departments

drawbacks.text: The funding and enforcement machinery is heavy: a new federally chartered commission with a $100 million two-year appropriation, monthly compliance audits, and fines reaching 30% of a school's total athletic revenue, costs that could pressure smaller programs and non-revenue sports like Olympic sports, which depend on money from football and basketball [S3].

The mandate to share 50% of revenue in big-money divisions, on top of trust fund contributions, is a large fixed cost on athletic departments, and critics of such proposals argue it could lead schools to cut minor sports rather than reduce coach salaries, which the bill only nudges at rather than requires [S3].

The Commission is structured as a federally chartered corporation that is not a federal agency yet wields enforcement power, subpoena authority, and rulemaking, an unusual design that drew constitutional questions about delegating government authority to a private-like body [S3].

Support was minimal even among Democrats: the bill had one cosponsor besides its sponsor and never received a hearing in either committee, suggesting it was a statement bill rather than near-term legislation [S4][S5].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the athletes themselves the benefits are substantial: income rights, guaranteed scholarships, injury coverage, and safety standards, at a price paid almost entirely by wealthy athletic programs, not taxpayers or other students. The honest objections are design ones, not purpose ones: the enforcement body is constitutionally awkward, the penalty structure could fall hardest on the smaller programs that share football money with Olympic sports, and the bill's sweeping scope made it easy to dismiss. Its main practical weakness was political: it arrived in the last days of a Congress with almost no cosponsors and no path to a vote.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced on December 18, 2020, two weeks before the Congress ended, and was referred to the Education and Labor and Energy and Commerce committees, where it sat with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote before the term expired [S1][S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Janice Schakowsky introduced the College Athletes Bill of Rights on December 18, 2020, with Rep. Steve Cohen as the only cosponsor [S1][S3][S4].
The bill was referred to two committees, Education and Labor and Energy and Commerce; neither took any further action on it [S1][S5].
The 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, sixteen days after introduction, so the bill received no vote in either chamber and expired [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The college athletics establishment — the NCAA, conferences, and major athletic departments — kept the existing system where athletes cannot be paid beyond scholarships, at least from this bill. The timing mattered: by mid-2021, after state NIL laws and litigation forced the issue, the NCAA changed its rules to let athletes profit from name, image, and likeness deals, though revenue sharing and injury trust funds like this bill proposed never materialized.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The NCAA and major college athletic departments

for.name: Rep. Janice Schakowsky
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to two committees in the closing days of the Congress

for.name: Rep. Steve Cohen
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the only additional supporter in the House

against.name: House committee leadership
against.role: Chairs of the Education and Labor and Energy and Commerce committees
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill before the Congress ended; the record shows no action after the December 18 referral

against.name: NCAA and major college athletics
against.role: Governing body and athletic departments affected by the bill
against.what_they_did: The bill would have redirected a large share of their revenue to athletes and imposed penalties on them; the NCAA had long opposed paying college athletes beyond scholarships, though it was under pressure from state laws and litigation at the time

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; the bill's only recorded support came from two House Democrats, and there is no record of Republican or broader Democratic positions on the bill itself.

industries.note: The bill would fine associations up to $250,000 per violation, force them to distribute revenue royalties to athletes, and strip their power to restrict athlete earnings, ending their role as the gatekeeper of unpaid amateurism. Their financial interest ran against the athletes the bill served.

industries.industry: College athletic departments (major football and basketball programs)
industries.note: Departments in big-money divisions would owe up to 50% of program revenue to athletes, 2.5-4% to the medical trust fund, and face fines of 15-30% of revenue for violations of the rights or safety provisions. These costs would come directly out of the revenue their athletes generate.

industries.industry: Sports marketing, licensing, and athlete representation
industries.note: Endorsement rights for hundreds of thousands of athletes would create a large new licensing market, and agents would gain a federal certification system through the new Commission. Athletes and this industry benefit together here, with the bill requiring the schools and NCAA to step out of the middle.
